name: Nigerian Jollof Rice
description: Jollof rice, a tomato-and-pepper rice cooked down until the grains take on real color and a faint smokiness, is one of West Africa's most fiercely defended dishes - real jollof depends on a proper tomato-pepper base blended and fried down before the rice ever goes in, not just rice simmered in tomato sauce. Scotch bonnet isn't a distinct item here, so jalapeño stands in, though it's far milder and lacks scotch bonnet's specific fruity heat.

ingredients_full.note: half for the base, half sliced

ingredients.note: half for the base, half sliced

steps_detailed: Blend the tomatoes, bell pepper, jalapeño, and half the onion into a smooth puree.
Brown the chicken in the oil, 6-7 minutes, then set aside.
Fry the remaining sliced onion in the same oil, 3-4 minutes, then add the tomato paste and cook 2 minutes to deepen its color.
Add the blended puree and simmer uncovered 15-18 minutes, stirring occasionally, until it reduces and darkens - this step is what gives jollof its real depth, not a shortcut to skip.
Stir in the rice, coating every grain in the sauce, then add the broth, bay leaf, and chicken.
Cover and cook on low heat 20-25 minutes without stirring, until the rice is tender and the bottom develops a faint char - the prized 'party jollof' crust.
Rest 5 minutes before fluffing and serving.

name: Nigerian Egusi Soup
description: Egusi soup, thickened with ground melon seeds, is a defining Nigerian dish - real egusi seeds, not a generic nut or seed substitute, are what give it its distinctive texture and nutty flavor.
steps_detailed: Brown the beef with the onion, 6-7 minutes.
Mix the ground egusi with a few tablespoons of water into a thick paste.
Heat the oil and fry spoonfuls of the egusi paste, breaking them into small lumps, 5-6 minutes, until they turn slightly golden - this step is what gives real egusi soup its characteristic texture.
Add the tomatoes and jalapeño, and simmer 10 minutes.
Add the beef and 1 cup water, and simmer 12-15 minutes.
Stir in the spinach in the last 3 minutes until just wilted.

name: Nigerian Suya Skewers
description: Suya, grilled meat coated in a dry peanut-and-spice rub called yaji, is one of Nigeria's most beloved street foods - real ground peanuts are what give the crust its texture, distinct from a simple spice rub alone.

ingredients_full.ingredient: Peanuts, all types, dry-roasted, with salt

ingredients.ingredient: Peanuts, all types, dry-roasted, with salt

steps_detailed: Mix the ground peanuts with the ginger, paprika, and chili powder into a dry rub (yaji).
Toss the sliced beef in the oil, then coat thoroughly in the yaji rub.
Thread onto skewers and grill over high heat, turning, 6-8 minutes, until charred at the edges.

name: Nigerian Pounded Yam
description: Pounded yam, real yam boiled and pounded until smooth and stretchy, is one of Nigeria's most essential starchy staples, traditionally eaten as a smooth accompaniment to soup - real yam is a distinct tuber from sweet potato, with a starchier, firmer texture.
steps_detailed: Boil the yam in salted water 20-25 minutes until completely fork-tender.
Drain well, then pound or mash vigorously until smooth, stretchy, and free of lumps - a mortar and pestle gives the real, elastic texture, though a sturdy masher works as a home approximation.

name: Nigerian Moin Moin
description: Moin moin, a steamed bean pudding made from real black-eyed peas blended smooth, is a beloved Nigerian side, traditionally steamed in wrapped leaves or small containers.

ingredients_full.ingredient: Cowpeas (blackeyes), immature seeds, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt

ingredients.ingredient: Cowpeas (blackeyes), immature seeds, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt

steps_detailed: Blend the cowpeas, bell pepper, and onion with a little water into a smooth, thick batter.
Whisk in the egg and oil.
Pour into small heatproof cups or ramekins.
Steam over simmering water 35-40 minutes until firm and set all the way through.

name: Nigerian Akara
description: Akara, fried black-eyed pea fritters, is a beloved Nigerian breakfast street food - whipping air into the batter before frying is what gives real akara its characteristic light, fluffy interior.

ingredients_full.ingredient: Cowpeas (blackeyes), immature seeds, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt

ingredients.ingredient: Cowpeas (blackeyes), immature seeds, cooked, boiled, drained, without salt

steps_detailed: Blend the cowpeas with the onion and jalapeño and a splash of water into a thick batter.
Whip the batter vigorously by hand for a few minutes to work air into it - this step is what makes real akara light rather than dense.
Drop spoonfuls into hot oil and fry, turning, 4-5 minutes per batch, until deeply golden and cooked through.

name: Nigerian Efo Riro
description: Efo riro, a rich spinach stew built on a proper tomato-pepper base, a Nigerian staple served alongside rice or a starchy swallow like pounded yam.
steps_detailed: Blend the tomatoes, bell pepper, jalapeño, and half the onion into a smooth puree.
Brown the beef with the remaining onion, 6-7 minutes.
Add the blended puree and simmer 12-15 minutes until it reduces and deepens in color.
Stir in the spinach and cook 3-4 minutes until just wilted.

name: Nigerian Pepper Soup
description: Pepper soup, a light, intensely spiced broth, is a Nigerian comfort food often served to those feeling under the weather - real pepper soup spice blends often include uziza and calabash nutmeg, which aren't distinct items here, so this leans on more widely available warming spices instead.
steps_detailed: Simmer the chicken in the broth with the jalapeño, ginger, and black pepper for 25-30 minutes until the chicken is very tender and the broth is well infused.
steps: Simmer the chicken in the broth with the jalapeño, ginger, and black pepper for 25-30 minutes until the chicken is very tender and the broth is well infused.

name: Nigerian Ofada Rice with Ayamase
description: Ayamase, also called designer stew, is a green-pepper stew traditionally paired with ofada rice, a specific local Nigerian rice variety - basmati stands in here for the rice, a reasonable but distinct substitute.
steps_detailed: Blend the green bell pepper and jalapeño into a coarse puree.
Heat the oil until quite hot and fry the pepper puree, stirring often, 12-15 minutes, until it darkens - real ayamase depends on this long fry to mellow the raw pepper bite.
Add the onion and beef, and cook 8-9 minutes until the beef is browned through.
Cook the rice separately and serve the stew over it.

name: Nigerian Puff Puff
description: Puff puff, deep-fried balls of slightly sweet dough, is one of Nigeria's most beloved snacks - real puff puff is yeast-leavened, giving it a light, slightly tangy character; yeast isn't a distinct item here, so baking powder stands in for a faster, less complex rise.
steps_detailed: Whisk the flour, sugar, and baking powder with warm water into a thick, smooth batter.
Let sit 10 minutes to hydrate.
Drop spoonfuls into hot oil and fry, turning, 4-5 minutes per batch, until deeply golden.

name: Nigerian Chin Chin
description: Chin chin, small pieces of sweet, crunchy fried dough, a beloved Nigerian snack especially at parties and celebrations.
steps_detailed: Mix the flour, sugar, butter, and egg into a firm dough.
Roll out and cut into small squares or strips.
Fry in batches, turning, 4-5 minutes, until deeply golden and crunchy all the way through.

name: Nigerian Meat Pie
description: The Nigerian meat pie, a flaky pastry filled with spiced ground meat and vegetables, is a beloved bakery staple distinct from other countries' meat pies in its specific curry-forward filling.
steps_detailed: Cut the butter into the flour with a splash of cold water until it forms a firm dough. Chill 20 minutes.
Brown the beef with the carrot, potato, and curry powder, 8-9 minutes, until the vegetables are just tender.
Roll out the dough and cut into rounds, spoon the filling onto one half of each round, fold over, and crimp the edges to seal.
Brush with the egg wash and bake at 375F (190C) for 25-28 minutes until deeply golden.

name: Nigerian Fried Rice
description: Nigerian fried rice, colored and flavored with real curry powder and a mix of chopped vegetables, is distinctly different from Chinese-style fried rice, often served alongside jollof rice at parties.

Add the curry powder and cook 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the cold rice and chicken, and stir-fry over high heat 5-6 minutes, breaking up clumps, until everything is well coated and heated through.

name: Nigerian Fish Stew
description: A tomato-pepper fish stew, built on the same real base as jollof and efo riro, a common Nigerian home-cooking staple.
steps_detailed: Blend the tomatoes, bell pepper, and jalapeño into a smooth puree.
Fry the onion in the oil 3-4 minutes, then add the puree and simmer 15 minutes until it deepens in color.
Add the fish and simmer 8-10 minutes until just cooked through.

name: Nigerian Dodo (Fried Plantain)
description: Dodo, ripe plantain sliced and fried until caramelized, a beloved Nigerian side dish, especially alongside jollof rice or beans.
steps_detailed: Fry the plantain slices in the oil over medium heat, turning once, 3-4 minutes per side, until deeply caramelized.

name: Nigerian Okra Soup
description: Okra soup, thickened by okra's natural sliminess rather than a starch, a genuine Nigerian home-cooking staple often paired with a swallow like pounded yam.
steps_detailed: Brown the beef in the oil, 6-7 minutes.
Add the tomatoes and jalapeño, and simmer 8-10 minutes.
Add the okra and simmer 6-8 minutes until tender - the soup should thicken naturally from the okra itself.

name: Nigerian Zobo Drink
description: Zobo, a hibiscus drink, is a beloved Nigerian non-alcoholic beverage, often flavored with ginger and pineapple.
steps_detailed: Warm the brewed hibiscus tea with the ginger for 5 minutes to infuse.
Stir in the sugar until dissolved, then chill.
Serve over ice with pineapple chunks.

name: Nigerian Groundnut Soup
description: Groundnut soup, built on real ground peanuts, a rich, nutty soup found across Nigeria and the wider West African region.
